In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a rationalized approach to size measurements of NMs and their characterization by different analytical methods.
the question of how to interpret size measurements by AFM, DLS, and FlFFF in a more consistent and rational way.
the question of how the measured size of NMs depends on the technique applied and how these results can be compared.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
DLS is not a suitable tool for size characterization of NMs.

the particle height measured by AFM is the closest to the true particle size, whereas DLS and FlFFF-UV should be used with caution, particularly for polydisperse samples and permeable particles, respectively.

DLS and FlFFF are suitable techniques for the size characterization of nanomaterial suspensions, but the results should be interpreted with care, and the measured sizes should not be used for risk assessment purposes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the size of a NM is not only a material property but is also a technique-dependent parameter.
AFM is a reliable and accurate technique for size determination, but it requires a sample preparation protocol and that the measured sizes should be interpreted with caution.

the size of NMs can vary significantly, even when measured by the same technique, and that a thorough analysis of the measured size distribution, including the particle shape and structure, is needed for the correct interpretation of the measured size by different techniques and for the correct comparison between different studies.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the measured size by a specific technique is not necessarily the most relevant size to be used for hazard identification, as it is dependent on particle structure, sample preparation, and polydispersity of the samples.
the size of NMs measured by AFM is the closest to the actual particle size and that the size measured by DLS is the least accurate, especially when polydispersity is high.
polydispersity and particle structure should be considered when evaluating NM sizes.
